newsitem.title: USA: NYMEX crude ends off but recovers from 9-month low.
newsitem.headline: NYMEX crude ends off but recovers from 9-month low.

text.p: NYMEX crude settled lower Monday but recovered from its lowest level in nine months on a late round of short covering.
"It was all short covering on little volume. The (calendar) spreads are still weak," said a New York dealer, noting crude was still vulnerable to the downside.
April crude ended off five cents a barrel at $20.25 a after falling to $19.96, its lowest level since June 26, 1996 when it hit a session low of $19.85.
The April/May spread thinned to 22 cents from 26 cents Friday.
"I still think we will take a peek below $20.00. Between $19.50 and $20.00 will be the moment of truth," said William Brown, president of trading firm W.H. Brown & Co in New York.
Brown said oil prices may bottom in that range before heading higher, led by gasoline which typically rallies in the spring in anticipation of peak demand during the summer.
The downtrend in oil prices has already lasted for more than a month, lopping 20 percent off crude and heating oil prices. Last week, the price of prompt crude lost more than $1.00 a barrel.

April heating oil ended off 0.26 cent at 53.18 cents a gallon, shrugging off forecasts of colder weather for the northeastern United States since winter was just about over after being relatively mild. The Northeast is the largest heating oil market in the world.
Besides from poor heating oil demand, heavy refinery maintenance has cut crude usage when gasoline demand is in a seasonal trough.
April gasoline ended off 0.79 cent a gallon at 61.77 cents. The April gasoline-to-crude crack spread fell to $5.65 a barrel from $5.98 Friday.
Although there was talk of significant gasoline imports from Europe, some cash traders said the imports were going to Canada and Latin America and not to the New York Harbor.
Meanwhile, crude prices would need to firm before gasoline can enjoy its seasonal rise, traders said.
"Gasoline can't rally without crude. We should be out of (refinery) turnaround by the end of March and crude runs should go higher," said Brown.
But, looming over crude was the reality that lower crude prices meant increased Iraqi exports.
In December, the United Nations eased sanctions against Iraq and allowed the country to export $2 billion worth of oil every six months, on a renewable basis, in exchange for humanitarian aid.
Because the export amount is linked to the dollar value and not the amount of barrels, lower crude prices mean a rise in volume.

Still, the economic sanctions imposed on Baghdad since its August 1990 invasion of Kuwait remain in place, retained by the U.N. Security Council on Monday during a review of the sanctions which is conducted every 60 days.

U.N. Special Commission chief Rolf Ekeus, who briefed the council on a recent trip to Baghdad, is still not satisfied Iraq has made full disclosure in the areas of long-range missiles, chemical and biological programs and related documents.
-- Harry Milling, New York Energy Desk, 212-859-1761
